summary: Defines standard link relation types that let a web service or API point to its own documentation, machine-readable descriptions, metadata, and status pages. Documentation links are aimed at people, while description links are aimed at software. A separate relation identifies a resource that reports the current status of the service.

eli5.summary: A website can put little signs on its doors saying where the instruction manual, the blueprint, and the weather report for the shop are kept. This is a set of standard names for those signs.

questions: how to link to api description
subtitle: Standard link relation types to point clients to service documentation, descriptions, and status

tldr.problem: Web APIs need to publish documentation for humans and machine-readable descriptions for software tools, but there is no standard way for clients to discover these resources when accessing a web service.
tldr.mechanism: This specification defines four new link relation types that services can include in their responses: service-doc for human documentation, service-desc for machine descriptions, service-meta for general service metadata, and status for service status resources.
tldr.outcome: Services can now advertise their documentation and status using standard typed links following RFC 8288, enabling clients and tools to automatically discover and consume this information.

today: RFC 8631 is an Informational specification that remains in active use. It is not on the Standards Track but enjoys wide adoption in the API ecosystem, with many services publishing documentation and descriptions via standard typed links.

sections.title: Discovering Service Information
sections.content:
Many resources on the Web are part of web services or APIs managed as a coordinated whole. When clients interact with these services, they often need to discover documentation, technical specifications, and operational status information. However, without a standard way to link to these resources, each service invents its own approach, and clients must hardcode knowledge of where to find this information.

RFC 8288 established a framework for typed links using standardized link relation types. This specification defines four new relation types that allow web services to advertise their documentation, technical descriptions, metadata, and status using this standard framework. Documentation targets human readers, while descriptions target software tools and code generators. Metadata encompasses any service-related information beyond documentation, and status resources convey service health and operational information.
sections.eli5: Imagine a store: browsers (humans) need to find the instruction manual on the bulletin board, while robots (software) need to find the blueprint. A standard set of signs means any browser or robot knows where to look.

sections.title: Two Kinds of Information
sections.content:
Service information falls into two broad categories. Documentation is primarily for human consumption and uses generic representations like HTML, PDF, or Markdown. It is often high-level and explanatory, putting the service in context and describing the general model and usage patterns.

Description is primarily for machine consumption and uses structured formats like XML, JSON, or RDF. It is detailed and technical, suitable for parsing by tools, code generators, and libraries. Examples include OpenAPI/Swagger descriptions for REST APIs or WSDL specifications for SOAP services.

These categories are not mutually exclusive: a single resource can serve both audiences, and a service typically has both high-level human documentation and detailed machine descriptions. Providing separate entry points for each lets services cater to different audiences without confusion. The specification also defines a service-meta link relation for general metadata that might not fit neatly into documentation or description categories, such as deployment information, privacy policies, or custom annotations.
sections.eli5: The store posts the customer guide in plain English on the wall, but also stores the inventory database in the computer system. Different visitors need different formats.

sections.title: The Link Relation Types
sections.content:
The service-doc link relation identifies resources that provide documentation primarily intended for human consumption. These typically are HTML pages, user guides, or tutorials.

The service-desc link relation identifies resources that describe the service in a machine-readable form. These could be OpenAPI specifications, WSDL files, JSON schemas, or other technical descriptions. The specification makes no assumptions about the format, allowing services to choose the representation that best fits their architecture.

The service-meta link relation points to resources containing general metadata about the service. This is a catch-all for service-related information beyond the specific scopes of documentation and description. For example, a service-meta link might point to a JSON document listing available languages, compliance certifications, pricing tiers, or links to privacy policies.

The status link relation identifies a resource representing the service's operational status. This can range from a simple status page confirming whether the service is operational, to a detailed dashboard showing subsystem status and incident history. The specification places no constraints on the representation; status pages can be designed for human consumption, machine consumption, or both.
sections.eli5: The store puts up four kinds of signs: one pointing to the customer guide (how to use), one pointing to the blueprint (technical details), one pointing to the schedule and policies (general info), and one showing if they're open today (status).

sections.title: Using Typed Links in Web Services
sections.content:
Services include these links in their HTTP responses using the Link header or embedded links in representations (such as HTML or JSON-LD). For example, a service's home page or metadata endpoint might include typed links with rel attributes like service-doc, service-desc, service-meta, or status pointing to corresponding resources.

When a client receives a response from the service, it can scan for these standardized link relations and automatically locate documentation, descriptions, or status resources. Tools can use service-desc links to download OpenAPI specifications and auto-generate client libraries. Monitoring systems can use status links to check service health. This approach enables service discovery and integration without hardcoding service-specific knowledge into clients.

Services that provide no distinction between documentation and description can instead use the existing service link relation type from RFC 5023, which is more generic.
sections.eli5: When you visit the store's website, you see links: 'Read our guide' (service-doc), 'Download our technical specs' (service-desc), 'Our policies' (service-meta), and 'Check if we're open' (status). Any robot can follow these standard signs.

sections.title: Applications and Benefits
sections.content:
Standard link relations enable several practical improvements to web services. API documentation portals can automatically discover and aggregate service-doc links from many services. API clients and SDK generators can discover and parse OpenAPI descriptions from service-desc links without manual configuration. Monitoring tools can automatically check all known services by following status links. Enterprise API governance can verify that all services publish required metadata via service-meta links.

The framework is flexible: services can use these link types with any documentation or description format they choose. A REST service might link to an OpenAPI specification, while a GraphQL service links to a GraphQL schema, and a legacy SOAP service links to WSDL. The standardized link relations make all these different services discoverable through a common mechanism.
sections.eli5: A robot can visit any store, see the standard signs, and know exactly what to read, download, or check. It doesn't have to learn each store's unique layout.
